[[File:Integral and Non-Integral graphs.svg|thumb|upright=1.15|The blue graph, [[cycle graph|{{mvar|C{{sub|4}}}}]], is one of the only integral [[cycle graph]]s, whose [[adjacency matrix]] has [[eigenvalue]]s <math>0, 0, 2, -2</math>. The red graph is ''not'' integral, as its eigenvalues are <math>0, -1, \frac{\sqrt{17} + 1}{2}, \frac{-\sqrt{17} + 1}{2}</math>.]]

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[graph theory]], an '''integral graph''' is a graph whose [[adjacency matrix]]'s [[Spectral graph theory|spectrum]] consists entirely of integers. In other words, a graph is an integral graph if all of the [[zero of a function|roots]] of the [[characteristic polynomial]] of its adjacency matrix are integers.<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=IntegralGraph|title=Integral Graph|mode=cs2}}</ref>

The notion was introduced in 1974 by [[Frank Harary]] and Allen Schwenk.<ref name=hs>{{citation
 | last1 = Harary | first1 = Frank | author1-link = Frank Harary
 | last2 = Schwenk | first2 = Allen J.
 | editor1-last = Bari | editor1-first = Ruth A. | editor1-link = Ruth Aaronson Bari
 | editor2-last = Harary | editor2-first = Frank
 | contribution = Which graphs have integral spectra?
 | doi = 10.1007/BFb0066434
 | mr = 0387124
 | pages = 45–51
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = Lecture Notes in Mathematics
 | title = Graphs and Combinatorics: Proceedings of the Capital Conference on Graph Theory and Combinatorics at the George Washington University, Washington, D.C., June 18–22, 1973
 | volume = 406
 | isbn = 978-3-540-06854-9 | year = 1974}}</ref>

==Examples==
*The [[complete graph]] ''K<sub>n</sub>'' is integral for all ''n''.<ref name=hs/>
*The only [[cycle graph]]s that are integral are <math>C_3</math>, <math>C_4</math>, and <math>C_6</math>.<ref name=hs/>
*If a graph is integral, then so is its [[complement graph]]; for instance, the complements of complete graphs, [[edgeless graph]]s, are integral. If two graphs are integral, then so is their [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian product]] and [[strong product of graphs|strong product]];<ref name=hs/> for instance, the Cartesian products of two complete graphs, the [[rook's graph]]s, are integral.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Doob | first = Michael
 | doi = 10.1016/0024-3795(70)90037-6
 | journal = [[Linear Algebra and Its Applications]]
 | mr = 285432
 | pages = 461–482
 | title = On characterizing certain graphs with four eigenvalues by their spectra
 | volume = 3
 | year = 1970| issue = 4
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> Similarly, the [[hypercube graph]]s, as Cartesian products of any number of complete graphs <math>K_2</math>, are integral.<ref name=hs/>
*The [[line graph]] of a regular integral graph is again integral. For instance, as the line graph of <math>K_4</math>, the [[octahedral graph]] is integral, and as the complement of the line graph of <math>K_5</math>, the [[Petersen graph]] is integral.<ref name=hs/>
*Among the [[cubic graph|cubic]] [[symmetric graph]]s the [[utility graph]], the [[Petersen graph]], the [[Nauru graph]] and the [[Desargues graph]] are integral.
*The [[Higman–Sims graph]], the [[Hall–Janko graph]], the [[Clebsch graph]], the [[Hoffman–Singleton graph]], the [[Shrikhande graph]] and the [[Hoffman graph]] are integral.
*A [[regular graph]] is [[Continuous-time quantum walk#Periodic graphs|periodic]] if and only if it is an integral graph.
*A [[walk-regular graph]] that admits [[Continuous-time quantum walk#Perfect state transfer|perfect state transfer]] is an integral graph. 
*The [[Sudoku graph]]s, graphs whose vertices represent cells of a Sudoku board and whose edges represent cells that should not be equal, are integral.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Sander | first = Torsten
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Electronic Journal of Combinatorics
 | mr = 2529816
 | page = Note 25, 7
 | title = Sudoku graphs are integral
 | url = https://www.combinatorics.org/Volume_16/Abstracts/v16i1n25.html
 | volume = 16
 | year = 2009
 | article-number = N25
 | doi = 10.37236/263
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref>
